newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Dry season takes hold in Ivory Coast.
newsitem.headline: Dry season takes hold in Ivory Coast.

text.p: Ivory Coast moved into its short dry season in the first part of July following heavy June rains that favoured the growth of 1997/98 main crop cocoa, weather and crop analysts said on Tuesday.
"There are still heavy rains in some cocoa areas but for most the dry season (July-August) is here," said a national weather centre analyst, adding that conditions were normal for the time of year.
Official national weather data for the first 10 days of July show rains averaged 16.7 mm at 10 monitored stations -- down from 83.2 and 147.4 in the previous two 10-day periods.
Rains on average fell on two of the first 10 days of July and had been concentrated around northern margins of cocoa and, particularly, coffee areas such as Man on the border with the savannah.
Southern and southwestern forest regions, where most cocoa is grown, received less.
"The June rain was abnormally high but beneficial," said one crop analyst.
He put average June rains in cocoa areas at just below 300 mm, against about 350 mm according to official data and his long-term average figure of 200 mm.
"According to my data it was the heaviest rainfall (in June) for 17 years," he added. That could help swell mid-crop bean sizes and had not damaged developing 1997/98 main crop pods," he said.
Weather centre analysts said in early July that June rains had been the heaviest for at least the past 10 years.

Rains in 1996 continued throughout July and August before a large 1996/97 crop, which had reached about one million tonnes by the start of the mid-crop. In 1995/96, Ivory Coast produced a record 1.2 million tonnes for the whole season.

Crop analysts told Reuters they expected a drier than normal July this year but said there was no reason to attribute that to a forecast El Nino weather system that has already brought climatic changes to other parts of the world.

"It could be a bit harder but it's just the dry season," said one, adding that the effects of El Nino were highly variable in West Africa and, in any case, were not expected to be felt until late 1997, if at all.
El Nino weather patterns have in the past been linked to drier than normal weather in West Africa.
A late 1997 El Nino dry period could affect the 1997/98 mid-crop (April-Sept) and, if prolonged, the start of the 1998/99 main crop, crop analysts have said.
Crop analysts have so far played down the possible effects of this year's El Nino for Ivorian cocoa and coffee.
Coffee analysts say the link between El Nino and African coffee crops is uncertain, although there had possibly been a negative impact in 1983.
Forecasters have said this year's El Nino could be as strong as the last major El Nino in 1982/83.
